translation:
Jivanji Maharaj went to meet Guru Gopaldasji. From there he went to Vrindavan and other places. It is written on page 412 of the genealogist's (vahivancha) ledger that Jivanji Maharaj held a feast (bhandaro) for the six schools of philosophy (shat-darshan) in Vrindavan, at the village of Puniyad, and also held a feast at the Galta seat in the village of Jaipur, and had a cow-shelter (goshala) built for his own bard (barot), giving woollen cloth (banat) worth 125 rupees in Samvat 1735. Thus Jivanji Maharaj went to Vrindavan twice.

Patan

_Patan padyo avatro, je Gokulno Kahaan. Sukhsagar sada Jivana, je diyo Sudama daan._ ||22|| Naamrup (He who was Kahaan [Krishna] of Gokul has taken avatar in Patan — he, Jivana, is forever an ocean of joy, who gave the gift [of devotion] to Sudama.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that the same Lord who was Bhagwan Krishna in Gokul has taken avatar in Patan as Bhagwan Padmanabh. He is forever the giver of the greatest joy. The same wealth of happiness that he gave to Sudama, he granted as the wealth of devotion to the one who was born as Sudama in the form of Adhyaruji.

_Krishna Kabiro avatarya, bhagat het Bharvaad. E jugal jodi bhaj Jivana, je Padmanabh avatar._ ||21|| Naamrup (Krishna and Kabir took avatar out of love for their devotees — Krishna as a Bharvaad [herdsman] and Kabir [Gopal] as a lovely maiden. Worship, O Jivana, that paired couple [of guru and disciple] who, at the time of the avatar of Padmanabh, had taken birth again as guru and disciple.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that for the welfare of devotees, Krishna took avatar as a Bharvaad (cowherd) and Kabir (Gopal) as a maiden; worship that paired bond of guru and disciple, who had taken avatar as guru and disciple at the time of the Padmanabh avatar.

In Vrindavan, during the childhood sport (baal-lila), when the companion boys of Vraj crowned Krishna king in play, Shiva went there and gave his blessing. On that occasion the Lord asked Radhaji for a necklace to give as a gift to Shiva, but Shiva would not accept a necklace made of pearls obtained through violence to a living creature. So Radhaji obtained a pearl from the waters of the Yamuna, other pearls were made from it, and the necklace was given to Shiva from these. At that time Kalahansa, the daughter of Bhoja Gurjar, stole three pearls from among those pearls. For this she was cursed to be born in the womb of a tree. That Kalahansa was the tamarind tree that grew in Patan. To redeem her, Jivanji Maharaj came to Patan indirectly for this purpose; therefore, in the Patan-vaadi (garden), next to Kabirji's tulsi planter, stands the tulsi planter of Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, in this same Patan garden. In this way Jivanji Maharaj brought about Kalahansa's redemption.

Adhyaruji Maharaj, having taken initiation from Bhagwan Padmanabh, composed twenty-eight kirtans. Jivanji brought us the devotion of these kirtans and gave it to us; therefore it is said:

_Patan aambo moriyo, zhintyo Zalawaad. Fal laagya chhe Malve, vedyo chhe Gujarat._ (The mango tree blossomed in Patan, was tended in Zalawad; its fruit grew in Malwa, and Gujarat had the good fortune to harvest it.)

The mango tree of Krishna-bhakti — the mango tree in the form of Padmanabh — appeared in Patan; the care of its young orchard (vadoliyu) took place in Kathiawad, in Dwarka-Sudamapuri, that is, Porbandar. Its fruit grew in Malwa in the form of devotees like Mira, and in Gujarat came the good fortune of harvesting that fruit.

The mango tree of Patan was in the form of Padmanabh; its devotion, in the form of the orchard of the twenty-eight kirtans, was tended by Sudama in the form of Adhyaru of Kathiawad.

The devotion of those kirtans was spread by Jivanji in Malwa, and in Gujarat the community of devotees gathered and preserved it.
